SECTION II - ENVIRONMENTAL SETTING WITHOUT THE PROPOSED ACTION
Rio Grande Basin
2.01 General. The Rio Grande basin extends from the Continental Divide in southern Colorado through New Mexico to Texas and the Gulf of Mexico. The basin is relatively long and narrow with a length of 1,820 miles and a maximum width of 235 miles. Its area is approximately 335,500 square miles of which 135,000 square miles are in the United States. Since nearly half of the basin yields no runoff to the river, the estimated productive area of the watershed is 176,333 square miles of which 88,968 square miles are in the United States. The total drainage area of the basin within Texas is 48,259 square miles of which 8,214 square miles do not contribute runoff. The Colorado River, Nueces River, and Nueces-Rio Grande Coastal basin adjoin the Rio Grande basin in Texas. The Pecos River and Devils River are the principal tributaries to the Rio Grande in Texas.
2.02 Climate. The climate of the Rio Grande basin between the Texas-New Mexico border and the Gulf of Mexico ranges from arid in the vicinity of El Paso to semi-arid and subtropical near the coast. At Del Rio, the January and July temperatures average 51° and 87° F, respectively, with an average freeze free period of 303 days. Precipitation gradually increases from a normal annual of 8 inches around El Paso, to a normal annual of 25 inches at Brownsville. Because of tropical storms and the accompanying torrential rains, large departures from the normal annual and monthly precipitation are common. Extremes in annual precipitation at Del Rio have ranged from a minimum of 4 inches to a maximum of 38 inches. Mean annual evaporation from lake surfaces in the basin is high as a result of the arid to semi-arid climate. The evaporation rate is approximately 80 inches annually near Del Rio. In almost all circumstances the annual lake evaporation will far exceed the annual precipitation. At Brownsville and Laredo, the prevailing wind is from the southeast and the mean wind speed is 12.3 mph. At El Paso, the prevailing wind is from the north.
2.03 Physiographic Description. From El Paso to the Gulf, a distance of about 1,240 river miles, the Rio Grande flows successively through three physiographic provinces: the Basin and Range, the Great Plains, and the Coastal Plain. Between El Paso and the Brewster-Terrell County line the Rio Grande flows through the Mexican Highlands section of the Basin and Range Province, constituting the southern extension of the Rockies. This section features isolated mountain ranges separated by aggraded desert plains. Along this reach, the Rio Grande flows through picturesque Santa Elena, Mariscal, and Boquillas Canyons which reach maximum depths of almost 2,000 feet.
2.04 From the Brewster-Terrell County line to Amistad Reservoir, the Rio Grande crosses the Edward Plateau section of the Great Plains physiographic province. In this reach the Rio Grande is confined to a continuous, generally steep-walled canyon cut in massive limestone strata of the Lower Cretaceous system. The plateau area consists of level-topped uplands of low relief with maturely dissected margins of moderate to strong relief. Near Del Rio the Rio Grande enters the West Gulf Coastal Plain section of the Coastal Plain physiographic province, and the steep-walled canyons above Del Rio give way to a relatively broad plain with gently sloping valley walls. Downstream from Del Rio the coastal plain section is formed on successively younger outcrop bands of upper Cretaceous, Tertiary, and Quaternary formations. The land surface slopes gently toward the Gulf. Minor scarps present elsewhere along the Texas Coastal Plain are not well defined in the Rio Grande basin area.
